content.title: Rational Functions: Vertical Asymptotes vs. Holes
content.overview: This lesson focuses on distinguishing between two types of discontinuities in rational functions: vertical asymptotes and holes (removable discontinuities). By factoring and simplifying rational expressions, you can determine whether a value that makes the denominator zero results in a vertical line the graph approaches or a single missing point.
learning_objectives: Factor polynomial numerators and denominators completely.
Identify holes by finding roots of factors that cancel out.
Identify vertical asymptotes by finding roots of denominator factors that remain after simplification.
Distinguish between removable and non-removable discontinuities.

sections.title: The Factor-Cancel-Asymptote Strategy
sections.content:
A rational function is a ratio of two polynomials. Discontinuities occur at any x-value that makes the denominator equal to zero. To classify these discontinuities, follow three steps: 1. Factor both the numerator and the denominator completely. 2. Cancel any common factors found in both the top and bottom. These canceled factors represent 'holes' (removable discontinuities). 3. Identify the remaining factors in the denominator. Setting these remaining factors to zero gives the equations for the vertical asymptotes.

![A flowchart showing the steps: Factor Numerator/Denominator, Cancel Common Factors, Canceled Factors = Holes, Remaining Denominator Factors = Vertical Asymptotes.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/275d77a2-7458-4365-945a-82637bea80c1-1786505849284-298.webp)

sections.title: Holes (Removable Discontinuities)
sections.content: A hole occurs at x = c if the factor (x - c) appears in both the numerator and the denominator. When you cancel this factor, the function behaves like the simplified version everywhere except at x = c, where the graph has a single undefined point. On a graph, this is often represented by an open circle.

sections.title: Vertical Asymptotes (Non-Removable Discontinuities)
sections.content: A vertical asymptote occurs at x = k if the factor (x - k) remains in the denominator after all possible cancellations. As x approaches k, the function's value grows toward positive or negative infinity. The line x = k is a vertical boundary that the graph never crosses.

worked_examples.question: Find the vertical asymptote(s) and hole(s) for the function f(x) = (x^2 - 4) / (x^2 - x - 6).
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Factor the numerator and denominator. The numerator x^2 - 4 is a difference of squares: (x - 2)(x + 2). The denominator x^2 - x - 6 factors into (x - 3)(x + 2). Step 2: Identify common factors. The factor (x + 2) appears in both. Cancel (x + 2) to find the hole. Setting x + 2 = 0 gives x = -2. There is a hole at x = -2. Step 3: Identify remaining denominator factors. The remaining factor is (x - 3). Setting x - 3 = 0 gives x = 3. Therefore, the vertical asymptote is the line x = 3.

common_mistakes: Assuming every value that makes the denominator zero is a vertical asymptote.
Forgetting to factor the numerator before identifying asymptotes.
Misidentifying the x-value of a hole (e.g., saying the hole is at x = 2 when the factor was x + 2).
Failing to simplify the expression fully before solving for asymptotes.
exam_tips: If the ACT asks for a vertical asymptote, always check if the denominator's root also makes the numerator zero.
Vertical asymptotes are written as equations (e.g., x = 3), not just numbers.
If a factor appears in the denominator with a higher multiplicity than in the numerator (e.g., (x-1)^2 in bottom and (x-1) in top), the root is still a vertical asymptote.
content.recap: To find discontinuities, factor everything. Canceled factors create holes; remaining denominator factors create vertical asymptotes.

knowledge_claims.content: A rational function is defined as the ratio of two polynomial functions.
The first step in identifying asymptotes or holes is to factor both the numerator and the denominator completely.
A hole exists at an x-value if its corresponding linear factor is present in both the numerator and the denominator and can be canceled.
A vertical asymptote exists at an x-value if its corresponding linear factor remains in the denominator after all common factors are canceled.
To find the x-coordinate of a hole, set the canceled common factor equal to zero and solve for x.
To find the equation of a vertical asymptote, set the remaining denominator factors equal to zero and solve for x.
Holes are considered removable discontinuities, while vertical asymptotes are non-removable infinite discontinuities.
It is a mistake to label a root of the denominator as a vertical asymptote if that same root also cancels with a factor in the numerator.
A vertical asymptote represents a line x = c that the graph approaches but never touches or crosses.
One can verify a vertical asymptote by testing x-values very close to the root to see if the function output becomes extremely large (positive or negative).
In the function f(x) = (x-1)/(x-1)(x-2), there is a hole at x=1 and a vertical asymptote at x=2.
The domain of a rational function excludes all x-values that make the original denominator zero, regardless of whether they are holes or asymptotes.

items.stem:
Practice form 1.
Which vertical asymptote does f(x)=1/(x-2) have?
A) x=2
B) y=2
C) x=-2
D) y=0 only
items.explanation: A vertical asymptote occurs where the denominator is zero.

items.explanation: A vertical asymptote occurs where the denominator is zero.

videoLesson.title: Verify Vertical Asymptotes Versus Holes
videoLesson.description: Recognize canceled factors as holes and remaining denominator roots as vertical asymptotes. Factor, cancel common factors, then set unreduced denominator factors equal to zero.
